To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the amount of residual function is a major determinant for recovery after ischemic hemiparesis, 2) patients with severe motor impairment after stroke are a heterogeneous group of patients with regard to their capacity for recovery, and 3) the initial motor deficit score can be used to identify patients who will recover well after stroke and those who will not recover.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of the degree of recovery of the motor system after stroke, and the factors that influence this recovery.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the initial motor score is the most important predictor for motor recovery after hemiparetic stroke.
the initial motor score is a good predictor for the course of motor recovery after stroke.
the degree of initial motor deficit is the best predictor of motor recovery after stroke, and the degree of motor recovery is the best predictor for the final outcome of hand function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the initial motor deficit is the best predictor of the degree of recovery of motor functions following a hemiparetic stroke.
motor function is not a linear function of the size of the lesion, but a function of the amount of spared motor cortex and of its connectivity.
a patient with a severe stroke is more likely to recover if he/she is able to move his/her hand at all, even if it is only slightly, in the first days following stroke.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the initial clinical motor status of the patient is the most important factor for predicting the degree of motor recovery.
patients with mild motor deficits recover almost completely, whereas severely affected stroke patients have a high probability to remain severely impaired for a long time.
motor recovery is a complex process and that it is not possible to predict the degree of recovery based only on the lesion size.
